summary: A survey and tutorial on connectionless data transmission, where each message is sent on its own without first setting up a connection. It was circulated for review ahead of a proposed US position urging that the OSI model include this style of communication.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 787 explains connectionless data transmission as sending one self-contained data unit without establishing a connection. It argues that OSI should support this alongside connection-oriented service because different applications need different behavior.

questions: where do connectionless services appear in osi
how does connectionless service differ from a connection
subtitle: A survey arguing that connectionless transmission complements connection-oriented service in OSI.

tldr.problem: The OSI Reference Model assumes connections for data exchange, but some applications and network technologies fit single-message transmission without a connection.
tldr.mechanism: The paper defines connectionless data transmission, compares it with connection-oriented transfer, surveys use cases, and discusses its role across OSI layers.
tldr.outcome: The paper argues that connectionless and connection-oriented services should be treated as complementary concepts in the OSI architecture.

today: RFC 787 was circulated for review as a working paper on OSI connectionless data transmission. Its cover says it had not been reviewed or approved by the relevant technical committee.

sections.title: Connectionless and Connection-Oriented Service
sections.content:
Connection-oriented interactions establish a connection, transfer related data units, and release the connection. The parties negotiate parameters first, and the connection can provide sequencing, recovery, and flow control.

Connectionless transmission sends one self-contained data unit in a single operation without prior negotiation or an assurance of delivery. The service does not relate messages or recover missing ones; an application may provide its own recovery.
sections.plainLanguage: A connection sets up an association before exchanging related data. Connectionless transmission sends a complete message without that setup and does not guarantee delivery.

sections.title: Applications for Connectionless Transmission
sections.content:
The paper identifies applications including periodic data collection, distributing one message to many destinations, short request-response exchanges, broadcast or multicast, redundant or time-sensitive data, local area networks, and network interconnection.

For these uses, the paper says the extra setup or recovery behavior of a connection can be unnecessary, while a self-contained message can be sent and routed independently.
sections.plainLanguage: Connectionless service can suit short questions and answers, broadcasts, sensor reports, and networks where each message can be handled on its own.

sections.title: Where the Service Fits in OSI
sections.content:
The paper discusses connectionless service across the seven OSI layers. It describes a natural role at the data link layer for LANs and at the network layer for routing independent packets.

It says session and presentation layers can pass a connectionless service through, while the application layer can expose it to applications and management functions. It proposes allowing conversion between connection-oriented and connectionless forms at the network, transport, and application layers.
sections.plainLanguage: The paper sees connectionless service as useful at several OSI layers. It especially proposes that applications, transport, and network layers may convert between the two service types.

sections.title: A Standards Discussion Document
sections.content:
The RFC was circulated to organizations involved or interested in international data communication standards for review. The paper was intended to inform a possible US position on changes to the OSI Reference Model.

The cover identifies the paper as a working paper that had not been reviewed or approved by the appropriate technical committee and did not represent a USA consensus at that time.
sections.plainLanguage: This document was circulated for comments as part of standards discussions. Its cover says it was a working paper, not an approved US consensus.
